items.title: Employment Gap Penalty Loop
items.content:
# Employment Gap Penalty Loop

An employment gap triggers automated downranking (mech.employment_gap_downranking_bias), which pushes the profile below keyword and qualification filters (mech.automated_keyword_qualification_filter); fewer interview invitations lengthen the gap, which in turn strengthens the downranking.

### Cycle Dynamics
This causal loop reinforces mechanisms across iterations:
- `mech.employment_gap_downranking_bias` amplifies `mech.automated_keyword_qualification_filter`
- `mech.automated_keyword_qualification_filter` amplifies `mech.employment_gap_downranking_bias`
items.summary: An employment gap triggers automated downranking (mech.employment_gap_downranking_bias), which pushes the profile below keyword and qualification filters (mech.automated_keyword_qualification_filter); fewer interview invitations lengthen the gap, which in turn strengthens the downranking.

specimens.label: The same profile, two cycles apart
specimens.context: same CV, same market, nine months between

lines.text: Cycle 1 — skills 91, domain 88, continuity penalty −22 (gap 14 months) → rank 57
Cycle 2 — skills 91, domain 88, continuity penalty −34 (gap 23 months) → rank 45

specimens.reading: Nothing in the work changed between the two rows. The only variable that moved is the one the penalty reads, and it moves because the penalty worked the first time.

specimens.label: Why the loop closes

lines.text: Downranking pushes the profile below the filter threshold.
Below the threshold there are no interviews.
No interviews means no offer, so the gap continues to grow.
A longer gap increases the penalty on the next application.

specimens.reading: Each step is a reasonable rule on its own. Together they form a cycle whose input is its own output.

perspectives.sees: Applications that return no reply at all, or a generic rejection, with the same CV and the same market as the cycle before.
perspectives.reads: Something in the profile moved between cycles, and the only thing that did move is the length of the break itself.
perspectives.does: Keeps applying, since applications are the only input available, and each month without an interview adds to the break the next application carries.

perspectives.sees: A ranked queue of several hundred applications against capacity to read a few dozen, on a requisition where time-to-fill is measured.
perspectives.reads: The order is a triage of a list that cannot be read end to end, not a judgement about anyone in it.
perspectives.does: Reads from the top down until the week's capacity is used, which is where the ranking becomes the decision.

perspectives.sees: A continuity feature computed from the dates in the parsed work history, shipping enabled by default.
perspectives.reads: It is one input among several in a ranking the buyer evaluates on throughput; whether a low-scored profile was unreadable rather than unqualified is not something the score records.
perspectives.does: Applies the penalty on every scoring pass and offers it as a setting the customer can switch off, which nothing in the default configuration prompts anyone to do.

items.title: Inflated-Requirements Search Saturation Loop
items.content:
# Inflated-Requirements Search Saturation Loop

Teams write inflated requirements that filter out strong generalists; the search stays open for months, recruiters tire of it, and the role is redefined mid-process.

### Cycle Dynamics
This causal loop reinforces mechanisms across iterations:
- `mech.inflated_requisition_requirements_vs_actual_team_needs` amplifies `mech.automated_keyword_qualification_filter`
- `mech.automated_keyword_qualification_filter` amplifies `mech.mid_process_role_requirement_redefinition`
- `mech.mid_process_role_requirement_redefinition` amplifies `mech.inflated_requisition_requirements_vs_actual_team_needs`
items.summary: Teams write inflated requirements that filter out strong generalists; the search stays open for months, recruiters tire of it, and the role is redefined mid-process.

specimens.label: The same requisition, rewritten twice

lines.text: Month 0 — 8 required technologies, 7+ years, staff-level scope. Applications: 340. Advanced to onsite: 2. Hired: 0.
Month 3 — search still open. Requirements rewritten upward: 10 technologies, 9+ years, plus formal lead experience.
Month 6 — search still open. Recruiter reassigned; team now covering the work with overtime.

specimens.reading: The response to a failed search was a narrower filter. The filter was the reason the search failed, which is the turn that makes this a loop.

specimens.label: Where the requirement came from

lines.speaker: Recruiter
lines.text: Do we really need nine years and Rust for this? The backlog is mostly billing endpoints.

lines.speaker: Hiring manager
lines.text: Nobody good has applied in three months. If we lower the bar we will get more of the same.

specimens.reading: The inference runs backwards: an empty pipeline is read as evidence that the bar is too low. That reading is what tightens the next iteration.

perspectives.sees: Three months of applications, two candidates reaching onsite, no hire, and the team covering the work with overtime.
perspectives.reads: The pipeline holds nobody the panel wanted, and a lower bar would add to the pool it has already turned down.
perspectives.does: Rewrites the requirements upward, adds the missing signal as a formal requirement, and reposts: a bad hire is recorded against them and an open search is not.

perspectives.sees: A requisition ageing past the time-to-fill it is measured on, and a requirements list that got longer at the rewrite.
perspectives.reads: The requirements belong to the hiring manager, who is the internal client for this search.
perspectives.does: Raises the question once, posts the revised text, and moves screening capacity to requisitions that can close.

perspectives.sees: A posting with ten required technologies, a nine-year threshold and a lead requirement, republished with a longer list than the version before it.
perspectives.reads: The list is either the bar or a wish, and the posting does not say which; the year thresholds are the part a filter can act on.
perspectives.does: Skips the posting or applies against a list they do not match, and never learns which of the requirements the screen enforced.

items.title: Take-Home Opportunity-Cost Saturation Loop
items.content:
# Take-Home Opportunity-Cost Saturation Loop

Candidates spend heavy hours on take-home assignments with no bounded scope, which leaves less time for applications, while reviewers work through the queue under evaluation fatigue.

### Cycle Dynamics
This causal loop reinforces mechanisms across iterations:
- `mech.interview_resource_scheduling_saturation` amplifies `mech.take_home_evaluation_fatigue_asymmetry`
- `mech.take_home_evaluation_fatigue_asymmetry` amplifies `mech.interview_resource_scheduling_saturation`
items.summary: Candidates spend heavy hours on take-home assignments with no bounded scope, which leaves less time for applications, while reviewers work through the queue under evaluation fatigue.

specimens.label: One month of a candidate calendar

lines.text: Take-home A: 14 hours. Take-home B: 11 hours. Take-home C: 16 hours.
Applications sent that month: 4 — down from 21 the month before.
Outcomes: two rejections after sub-ten-minute reviews, one no response, one still open.

specimens.reading: The hours are real and they come out of the same budget as the search itself. Fewer applications is not a change in motivation; it is arithmetic.

specimens.label: The same month from the reviewer side

lines.text: Submissions in the queue: 19 · Reviewer capacity: 2 hours per week
Median review time per submission: 6 minutes.
Reviewers report the assignments are too large to assess properly, and the scope is set by the same team.

specimens.reading: Both sides are short of the same thing. Larger assignments do not buy better signal — they buy shallower reads, which is what makes it a loop rather than a trade-off.

perspectives.sees: Assignments scoped at a few hours that take double-digit hours each, and rejections returned faster than the work can be read.
perspectives.reads: The hours come out of the same budget as the search itself, so each assignment is a bet placed against the applications not sent that week.
perspectives.does: Sends fewer applications and finishes the assignments already accepted, because the hours in them are already spent.

perspectives.sees: A queue of submissions and interviewer hours that are already committed to the sprint the role exists to relieve.
perspectives.reads: A larger assignment covers more of the job, and a full read of every submission is not available from the hours the team has.
perspectives.does: Keeps the scope, since a smaller assignment would decide less, and the reviews get the minutes left after the team's own delivery.

perspectives.sees: Candidates going quiet between the assignment being sent and the work coming back, and time-to-fill running on the requisition.
perspectives.reads: A stage where the pipeline stalls is a reason to put more people into it, not a reason to remove the stage.
perspectives.does: Sends reminders and reopens sourcing, which puts more submissions into the same review queue.
